n: This chapter is Matthew’s fourth major discourse, on life in the community of disciples. It begins with the disciples asking who will rank highest in God’s kingdom.
Jesus answers with an object lesson: he calls a small child and places the child in the middle of the group.

f.g: Children had little status in that society — which is the point.

n: Unless we change and become like little children — humble, trusting, teachable — we won’t enter the kingdom at all, let alone be great in it.
True greatness in God’s kingdom is humility, the opposite of the status-seeking in the disciples’ question.
Welcoming a humble child for Jesus’s sake is welcoming Jesus himself.
Leading a believing “little one” into sin is so serious that drowning with a heavy millstone around one’s neck would be preferable.

f.g: Here: cause to stumble into sin or lose faith.
A large grinding stone turned by a donkey — far heavier than a hand mill.

n: In a fallen world temptations will come, but the person who causes them bears responsibility.
Vivid exaggeration: whatever leads you into sin, remove it decisively. Being spiritually whole is worth any sacrifice.
Even the eye — what we choose to look at — must be guarded if it leads us into sin.
Never look down on these little ones; they are so precious that their angels have direct access to the Father.

f.g: despise = look down on, treat as worthless.

n: Jesus came specifically to rescue the lost. (Some ancient manuscripts lack this verse; a similar line appears in Luke 19:10.)

f.w: to save that which was lost

n: A shepherd with a hundred sheep goes searching the hills for the one that wandered off.
Finding it brings special joy. Every individual matters to God.

f.w: he rejoiceth more of that sheep

n: The Father doesn’t want even one of his little ones to be lost.
When someone wrongs you, go privately and talk with them first. The goal is reconciliation — “gaining” your brother — not winning.
If that fails, bring one or two others along, following the law’s principle of multiple witnesses.
If the person still won’t listen, bring it to the congregation. If they reject even that, they place themselves outside the fellowship.

f.g: Greek ekklēsia — the congregation of believers.
A Gentile, an outsider to the covenant.

n: Jesus extends to the apostles the binding and loosing authority promised to Peter — their decisions, made with his authority, are honored in heaven.

f.w: Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth

n: When disciples unite in prayer for something, the Father hears and answers.

f.w: if two of you shall agree

n: Even the smallest gathering in Christ’s name has his presence.

f.w: where two or three are gathered together in my name

n: Peter asks how many times he must forgive someone. Seven times seemed generous — some rabbis taught three.
Jesus answers: seventy times seven — in other words, without keeping count.

f.g: Possibly “seventy-seven times”; either way, limitless. It reverses Lamech’s boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge.

n: Jesus tells a parable about a king settling accounts with his servants.
One servant owes ten thousand talents — an impossibly huge sum, deliberately exaggerated. It pictures our unpayable debt to God.

f.g: A talent was about 6,000 days’ wages; this debt equals roughly 60 million days of labor.

n: Unable to pay, he faces being sold with his family into slavery — a real practice for debts in the ancient world.
The servant begs for patience and promises to repay everything — something he could never actually do.
Moved with compassion, the king doesn’t just extend the deadline — he cancels the entire debt. That is grace.
The forgiven servant then finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii — real money, but tiny by comparison — and starts choking him.

f.g: A hundred denarii; a denarius was a day’s wage — roughly 600,000 times less than his own debt.

n: The fellow servant pleads with nearly the same words the first servant had used.
He refuses and has the man jailed until he pays, forgetting the mercy he himself just received.

f.g: Debtors’ prison; family or friends might raise money to free the prisoner.

n: The other servants are distressed and report everything to the king.
The king summons him and calls him wicked: he was forgiven everything simply because he asked.
The key question of the parable: having received such mercy, shouldn’t he show mercy too?

f.w: even as I had pity on thee

n: The angry king hands him over to the jailers until his debt is paid — which can never happen.
Jesus applies it plainly: if we won’t forgive others from the heart, we cut ourselves off from God’s forgiveness.
